newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA METALS-Hindalco to lead revival in aluminium.
newsitem.headline: INDIA METALS-Hindalco to lead revival in aluminium.

text.p: India's Hindalco Industries Ltd is all set to cash in on a revival of the domestic aluminium industry with an anticipated rise in global demand and prices, analysts and industry leaders said on Thursday.
The optimism springs from strong economic growth in the United States and Japan and Europe's improving economies.
The analysts said a cutback in Russia's aluminium exports following growing local consumption and prospects of meagre global capacity expansion would further tighten supplies.
"The worse is over on the global price front," said Hindalco president S.P. Shorewala.
"Prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are expected to move upwards, which will benefit the Indian industry," he said.
India imports the bulk of its requirement of non-ferrous metals, except aluminium, in which it is surplus. But aluminium imports are allowed under its current liberal trade policy.

India has four major aluminium companies, Hindalco and Indian Aluminium Company Ltd (Indal), both in the private sector, and the state-owned National Aluminium Company Ltd (Nalco) and Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd.
Hindalco is rated India's most cost-efficient aluminium company in the private sector.
India has an installed capacity of 670,000 tonnes of aluminium. It annually produces about half a million tonnes of the metal. In 1995/96 (April-March) it exported about 70,000 tonnes of aluminium.
Hindalco produced 167,272 tonnes of aluminium in 1996/97, down from 175,398 tonnes in the previous year.
Analysts said the performance of all the firms was affected in 1996/97 (April/March) due to low LME prices, domestic power shortages and poor demand from user industries.
"The outlook for the aluminium industry for 1997/98, however, is positive," said Yeshwant Kini, an analyst from the securities firm Natwest Markets.

Kini said he would expect domestic demand to grow at 5.5 percent in 1997/98 against 4.5 percent in 1996/97, when India posted industrial growth of 6.7 percent against 11.6 percent in the previous year.
Analysts said they would expect Hindalco to do well in 1997/98. The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) has projected 12 percent industrial growth in the current fiscal year.

In 1996/97, Hindalco reported a net profit of 3.91 billion rupees against 4.01 billion rupees in the previous year. It also posted lower net sales of 11.57 billion rupees in 1996/97 compared with 12.52 billion in the previous year.
Analysts said Hindalco's expansion plans and increased volumes of added-value products, aided by firm LME prices should help the company improve its performance from 1997/98 onwards.
The company said it planned to expand its alumina capacity to 450,000 tonnes from the present 350,000 tonnes in 1997/98.
"The process of adding the new capacity will begin from August," said Hindalco's Shorewala.
Natwest's Kini said he would expect the value-added products in Hindalco's output to rise to 52 percent in 1997/98 from 42 percent in the previous year and to 56 percent in 1998/99.
"The company's outlook in the current year is bright. We're bullish on it and we have put the share on our buy list," said an analyst from a foreign securities firm.
Nalco chairman S.N. Johri said that in 1996/97 low LME prices spurred imports of aluminium to meet domestic demand.
"But this year, LME prices are higher," he said. "Therefore imports will be less. Hence, the domestic demand has to be met by domestic supplies."
Analysts said they also expected the performance of Indal, plagued by power shortages and low metal output, to improve.
"We look for a higher earnings growth for Indal, driven mainly by higher internal metal production," one analyst said.
